title: The Hellenistic World
orientation: This chapter sets the historical stage for the rest of Part III: it explains how Alexander's conquests dissolved the world of the independent Greek city-state and created the 'Hellenistic' world of the third and second centuries B.C., a world of political disorder, specialized science, cosmopolitan mixing of peoples, and spreading superstition. Understanding this social collapse is essential background for why Hellenistic philosophy (Cynicism, Scepticism, Epicureanism, Stoicism) turns inward toward private virtue rather than outward toward civic life.
historical_background: Alexander conquered the Persian Empire between 334 and 324 B.C., founding Greek-style cities as far as Afghanistan and the Punjab. After his death (323 B.C.) his empire fractured among his generals' dynasties: the Ptolemies in Egypt (capital Alexandria), the Seleucids in Asia (eventually centered on Antioch), and Antigonid Macedon in Europe. Two centuries of dynastic warfare, mercenary armies, social unrest, and currency/debt instability followed, until Rome absorbed the Hellenistic kingdoms one by one, finishing with Egypt after Cleopatra's death.
philosophical_problems: How does the collapse of the self-governing city-state change what philosophy is for?
Can a cosmopolitan, mixed-population empire sustain the same civic virtues as the old polis?
Why do periods of political chaos and insecurity tend to produce either fatalism (belief in Fate/astrology) or its opposite, a cult of blind luck (Fortune)?
What made Alexandria able to sustain first-rate specialized science while producing no new universal philosophy comparable to Plato or Aristotle?

philosophers_discussed.name: Alexander the Great
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Not a philosopher himself, but the central historical actor: his conquests and his policy of deliberately fusing Greeks and 'barbarians' (including intermarriage) planted, in practice, the cosmopolitan idea of a single human community that Stoic philosophy later formulated in theory.

philosophers_discussed.name: Aristotle
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Quoted briefly as representative of the ordinary Greek assumption that Greeks alone combine spirit and civilization, and that non-Greeks could rightly be enslaved -- the attitude Alexander's policies began to erode.

schools_discussed: Epicureanism and Stoicism (their founding placed in this period, treated fully in later chapters)
Scepticism as a formal doctrine (founding placed in this period)
Alexandrian mathematics and science (Euclid, Archimedes, Aristarchus, Apollonius, Eratosthenes)

core_concepts.name: The Hellenistic Age as a distinct period
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Russell divides Greek antiquity into three phases: free but disorderly city-states (to Philip/Alexander), Macedonian domination marked by subjection and disorder (the 'Hellenistic' age proper), and finally Roman rule, which brought subjection but also order. The Hellenistic age is the middle phase.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The period from Alexander's conquests (334-323 B.C.) to the final Roman absorption of the Macedonian successor kingdoms (ending with Egypt in 30 B.C.), during which Greek culture spread across a vastly enlarged, politically fragmented world under Macedonian dynasties.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It is the incubator of Epicureanism, Stoicism, and formal Scepticism, and of the diffusion of Greek science; it also prepared, in Russell's view, the psychological ground for Christianity by turning philosophy toward individual salvation.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Begins with Alexander's campaigns of 334-324 B.C. against the Persian Empire.
examples: The Ptolemaic kingdom of Egypt and its capital Alexandria
The Bactrian Greek kingdom under Menander
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Sets the social conditions (loss of civic power, chronic insecurity) that Russell says produced the individualist, salvation-oriented philosophies of the Cynics, Sceptics, Epicureans, and Stoics discussed in the following chapters.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly political: it is defined by the transition from city-state self-government to dynastic empire.

core_concepts.name: Cosmopolitanism (the idea of mankind as a whole)
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Once Alexander began treating Greeks and non-Greeks as potential equals -- marrying Persian nobility, ordering his officers to do the same, founding mixed cities -- thoughtful people started to conceive of humanity as one community rather than a patchwork of rival city-states and superior/inferior races.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The view that human loyalty and moral concern extend, in principle, to all mankind rather than being confined to one's own city or ethnic group; in philosophy this view is first fully worked out by the Stoics.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell treats it as the single most important social legacy of Alexander's reign, and as the historical seed of Stoic universalism and, later, of Christian and modern conceptions of a common humanity.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Emerges in practice from Alexander's policy of fusion (intermarriage, mixed garrison-cities) after his conquests, before it is formulated in theory.
core_concepts.associated_philosopher: Alexander the Great (in practice); the Stoics (in theory, treated in Ch. XXVIII)
examples: Alexander's own marriages to Persian princesses
His compelling his Macedonian officers to marry Persian noblewomen
Greek cities founded throughout Asia with mixed populations
objections: Plato and Aristotle had held it wrong to enslave Greeks but not barbarians -- the older, particularist view cosmopolitanism displaced
competing_positions: The traditional Greek view of a sharp superiority over 'barbarians', which Russell quotes Aristotle as expressing
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Directly anticipates the Stoic doctrine of the brotherhood of man (Ch. XXVIII) and, through the Stoics, later Christian and Roman legal ideas of natural human equality (Ch. XXIX).
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Political in origin (imperial policy of fusion), later absorbed into philosophy and religion.

core_concepts.name: Specialization of knowledge and activity
core_concepts.plain_explanation: In classical Athens a capable man was expected to be soldier, politician, and thinker all at once (Russell's examples: Socrates, Xenophon, Plato). In the Hellenistic world this stopped: soldiers were soldiers, mathematicians were mathematicians, administrators were administrators, and no one aspired to Aristotle's kind of universal competence.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The Hellenistic shift toward professional specialization in science, administration, the military, and philosophy, replacing the classical ideal of the all-round citizen-philosopher-statesman.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It explains, for Russell, why Alexandrian science (Euclid, Archimedes, Aristarchus, Apollonius) reached a technical level equal to anything earlier while philosophy after Aristotle produced no new universal system until the Neoplatonists five centuries later.
core_concepts.historical_origin: A consequence of Macedonian rule removing real political power from the citizen body of the old poleis, so that public life ceased to require an all-round competence.
examples: Euclid, Aristarchus, Archimedes, and Apollonius as pure mathematicians uninterested in philosophical originality
Uneducated Macedonian soldiers employing Greek experts for irrigation and drainage in Egypt
competing_positions: The earlier classical ideal, exemplified by Socrates (soldier and philosopher), Xenophon (general and writer), and Pythagorean mathematicians who sought to govern cities
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Follows directly from the loss of self-government in the Greek cities under Macedonian rule.

core_concepts.name: Political impotence and the retreat into private virtue
core_concepts.plain_explanation: When ordinary Greeks lost any real power over their own political fate -- power now lay with rival Macedonian generals and their armies -- serious-minded people stopped trying to reform the state and instead asked how an individual could stay virtuous, or at least undisturbed, in a world he could not control.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The historical-psychological condition, produced by the eclipse of the city-state, in which philosophy shifts its central question from 'how can we build a good state?' to 'how can the individual be happy or virtuous regardless of the state of the world?'
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell presents this shift as the single most important consequence of the Hellenistic collapse for the history of philosophy, directly producing Cynicism, Scepticism, Epicureanism and (for most of its history) Stoicism, and eventually preparing the ground psychologically for Christianity's gospel of individual salvation.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Produced by the destruction of the old Greek City States' independence under Philip and Alexander and the ensuing Macedonian wars.
examples: The general shift, described at the chapter's close, of philosophy from 'a pillar of fire going before intrepid seekers after truth' to 'an ambulance picking up the weak and wounded'
competing_positions: The classical civic-minded philosophy of Plato and Aristotle, still oriented to reforming or ruling the state
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Anticipates the entire subject matter of Chapters XXVI-XXVIII (Cynics, Sceptics, Epicureans, Stoics) and, ultimately, Christianity's this-worldly pessimism paired with other-worldly hope.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: This is Russell's central political-to-philosophical causal claim in the chapter.

core_concepts.name: Worship of Fortune and belief in astrological Fate
core_concepts.plain_explanation: With life made unpredictable by constant war, palace revolutions, and economic instability, people turned either to worshipping 'Fortune' (blind luck) or to astrology, which promised that the future, however grim, was at least fixed and knowable in advance.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Two complementary popular responses to Hellenistic insecurity: the cult of Tyche (Fortune/Luck) as an arbitrary power governing events, and the Chaldean/Babylonian doctrine of astrological determinism, which most people (and even most philosophers) held simultaneously without noticing the inconsistency.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Marks, for Russell, the point at which Greek rationalism began to be swamped by 'oriental' superstition, a process that continued until the triumph of Christianity.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Astrology reached the Greek world through Alexander's opening of contact with Babylon; Russell cites the Chaldean Berosus, who taught astrology at Cos.
examples: The Chaldean priest Berosus teaching astrology at Cos
Royal tombs (Ozymandias, Antiochus I) decorated with astrological symbols
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Astrology persists as a serious intellectual temptation for later Stoic philosophers (Ch. XXVIII) and other Hellenistic thinkers.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly religious; Russell treats it as the chief 'bad' side of the meeting of Greek and 'barbarian' cultures.

arguments.title: Why the new Macedonian disorder was worse than the old Greek disorder
arguments.philosopher: Bertrand Russell (historical judgment, not attributed to an ancient philosopher)
premises: The disorder of the old, free Greek city-states was tolerable because every citizen had a share in it (freedom plus disorder).
The disorder of the Hellenistic age was imposed on subject populations by incompetent Macedonian rulers who did not share power with them (subjection plus disorder).
Having no share in one's own political fate is worse than sharing in a disorder one can at least influence.
arguments.conclusion: The Macedonian age's disorder was 'far more so' intolerable than even the subsequent subjection to Rome, despite Rome's greater 'stupidity and brutality.'
arguments.explanation: Russell's point is not that Macedonian rule was more violent than classical Greek warfare, but that it combined the worst of both worlds: the instability of the old disorder without the compensating dignity of citizen participation. Roman rule, by contrast, was subjection but with order, which he treats as a real improvement in practice even though it ended Greek self-government entirely.
implications: Order, even imposed by a 'stupid and brutal' external power, can be preferable to participatory but chronic disorder.
This sets up Russell's generally positive assessment of the Roman peace in Chapter XXIX.

arguments.title: The essentially urban, commercial character of Greek civilization explains its fragility abroad
premises: Greek intellectual and commercial culture, from the Milesians onward, was carried by city-dwellers, not the surrounding rural population.

The new cities founded by Alexander were populated by adventurers from many different Greek regions, not by kin-based colonists from a single mother city, and were surrounded by unrelated 'barbarian' populations doing the agricultural labour.

A ruling minority that does not control its own food supply and land, and is not bound by kinship/tradition to its city, cannot form a durable political community (Russell's modern analogy: European treaty-port communities such as Hong Kong or Shanghai).
arguments.conclusion: None of Alexander's new cities, including Alexandria, formed a strong or lasting political unit, even though this instability suited the interests of the Macedonian kings who ruled over them.
arguments.explanation: Russell uses a direct historical analogy to nineteenth-century European colonial enclaves in Asia to argue that a commercial, non-agricultural ruling class transplanted onto a foreign population is inherently precarious, unlike the settled agricultural colonization of, e.g., North America.
implications: Explains why Hellenistic Greek culture spread widely in language and science but did not produce durable, self-governing political communities outside the older Greek homeland.

key_distinctions: Freedom-with-disorder (classical city-states) vs. subjection-with-disorder (Hellenistic kingdoms) vs. subjection-with-order (Rome)
Old kinship-based Greek colonies (bound to a mother city) vs. Alexander's new mixed 'adventurer' cities
Fortune/Luck (arbitrary chance) vs. astrological Fate (rigid, predictable necessity) as rival popular responses to insecurity
The classical ideal of the all-round citizen-statesman-philosopher vs. the Hellenistic reality of narrow specialization
connections_to_earlier_philosophers: Russell reaches back to the Milesian school and to Plato and Aristotle: the Milesians are cited as the origin of the pattern by which Greek science and philosophy were tied to rich commercial cities; Plato and Aristotle are cited (via Aristotle's remark on Greeks and barbarians) as holding the older, particularist view of Greek superiority that Alexander's cosmopolitan policy began to dissolve.
connections_to_later_philosophers: The chapter explicitly previews the Cynics and Sceptics (Ch. XXVI), the Epicureans (Ch. XXVII) and the Stoics (Ch. XXVIII), all said to be founded 'about the time of Alexander,' and frames the cosmopolitan idea of mankind as the direct forerunner of Stoic universalism.
political_social_context: The chapter is largely political history: Alexander's campaigns (334-324 B.C.), the division of his empire among the Ptolemies, Seleucids, and Antigonids, chronic dynastic warfare, mercenary armies, falling free wages amid competition from slave labour, rising prices, temple-banks controlling credit, and treaties (e.g., the League of Corinth, 335 B.C.) designed to prevent debt cancellation or land redistribution that might spark social revolution.
religion_science_culture_context: Alexandria becomes the center of specialized Greek mathematics and science (Euclid, Archimedes, Aristarchus, Apollonius, Eratosthenes); at the same time Babylonian/Chaldean astrology and magic spread into Greek culture, a development Russell judges to be, on balance, culturally harmful compared to the potential influence of more sophisticated Jewish, Persian, or Buddhist religious thought.
russell_presentation: Russell narrates the Hellenistic period as the pivotal hinge between the classical Greek world and Rome/Christianity. He credits Alexander, largely for reasons of practical necessity rather than idealism, with founding in practice the cosmopolitan idea of mankind that the Stoics would later formalize. He judges Hellenistic philosophy in general to represent a 'retreat' from the confident, civically engaged temper of Plato and Aristotle into private, individualist concerns, caused by ordinary Greeks' total loss of political power under Macedonian rule. He treats Alexandrian science as genuinely excellent but narrowly specialized, contrasts this favourably with the intellectual and moral 'chaos' of Hellenistic politics, and is notably harsher on the spread of Babylonian astrology and magic than on other Eastern religious influences, which he suggests could have been philosophically fruitful. He closes by quoting an assessment that Hellenistic philosophy became 'an ambulance following in the wake of the struggle for existence,' a line he clearly endorses as summarizing the age's mood.
critical_context: Historiographical note: Russell's contrast between Greek 'reason' and incoming 'barbarian' superstition, and his analogy between Hellenistic Greek cities and nineteenth-century European colonial treaty ports (Hong Kong, Shanghai), reflect early-twentieth-century assumptions about a civilizational hierarchy between Greek/European and 'Oriental' cultures. Later scholarship on the Hellenistic world (e.g., on Greco-Egyptian and Greco-Babylonian syncretism) generally treats this cultural mixing as more genuinely two-directional and productive than Russell's largely negative framing of 'barbarian' influence suggests.
key_takeaways: Russell divides Greek antiquity into three phases: free-and-disorderly city-states, subjected-and-disorderly Macedonian rule (the Hellenistic age proper), and subjected-but-orderly Roman rule.
Alexander's conquests (334-324 B.C.) and his policy of fusing Greek and non-Greek populations planted, in practice, the cosmopolitan idea of a single humanity that Stoicism later made explicit.

The loss of city-state self-government turned philosophy's central question from 'how do we build a good state?' to 'how can I be virtuous or happy regardless of the state of the world?' -- the theme of the next three chapters.
Hellenistic science (centered on Alexandria) reached a very high technical standard but became narrowly specialized rather than aiming, like Plato and Aristotle, at a universal philosophy.

Chronic political and economic insecurity produced two popular responses: cult worship of blind Fortune, and belief in astrological Fate imported from Babylon -- usually held inconsistently at the same time.
Russell judges the new Macedonian disorder as worse, in practice, than either the old civic disorder of free Greece or the later, more orderly subjection to Rome.
study_notes:
Read this chapter as scene-setting rather than as an argument in its own right: Russell is establishing the social and political facts that will explain, in the next three chapters, why post-Aristotelian philosophy looks so different in temper from Plato's and Aristotle's. The key move to notice is the causal chain he draws: loss of political self-determination -> retreat from public into private concerns -> philosophy redefined as personal therapy rather than civic architecture. When you reach the Cynics, Sceptics, Epicureans, and Stoics, keep asking how each school responds to the specific problem posed here: how to secure some kind of good (virtue, pleasure, tranquility) that does not depend on external, uncontrollable political fortune.

It is also worth noticing Russell's double-edged treatment of 'mixing' cultures: he treats the political/ethical effect of Greek-barbarian fusion (cosmopolitanism) as historically progressive, while treating the religious/intellectual effect (the spread of astrology and magic) as regressive. This asymmetry is itself worth questioning as you read -- it reflects Russell's own rationalist commitments as much as it reflects the historical evidence.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The period and culture of the Greek-speaking world after Alexander the Great's conquests, roughly 323 to 30 B.C., when Greek civilization spread across the Middle East and mixed heavily with local cultures.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The era following the death of Alexander the Great, characterized by the Macedonian successor kingdoms (Ptolemaic, Seleucid, Antigonid), a diffusion and internal transformation of Greek language and culture across a vastly enlarged geographic area, and the foundation of the Epicurean, Stoic, and formal Sceptical schools of philosophy.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The generals of Alexander the Great who fought over and divided up his empire after his death.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The rival Macedonian generals -- principally Ptolemy, Seleucus, and Antigonus -- whose dynasties partitioned Alexander's empire into the Ptolemaic, Seleucid, and Antigonid kingdoms after decades of civil war.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The idea that all human beings, not just members of one's own city or people, belong to a single moral community.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The doctrine that moral concern and citizenship extend in principle to all mankind rather than being confined by city or ethnicity; emerges in practice under Alexander and is systematized in theory by the Stoics.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The Greek goddess of luck or chance, worshipped increasingly as ordinary life came to feel unpredictable and uncontrollable.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The personification of arbitrary chance in Hellenistic religion, whose growing cult Russell reads as a symptom of the era's political and economic insecurity, existing in uneasy coexistence with the competing belief in astrological necessity.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The belief, imported from Babylon, that the movement of stars and planets determines or predicts human events and fates.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: A body of divinatory doctrine transmitted to the Greek world from Babylonian ('Chaldean') priestly tradition after Alexander's conquests, entailing a form of cosmic determinism that Russell notes most Hellenistic thinkers, including many Stoics, held alongside an inconsistent belief in Fortune.

questions.prompt: According to Russell, what three periods does the history of the Greek-speaking ancient world divide into, and what characterizes each?
questions.answer: (1) The period of the free City States, ended by Philip and Alexander -- freedom and disorder. (2) The Macedonian domination (the Hellenistic age proper), ended by Rome's annexation of Egypt -- subjection and disorder. (3) The Roman Empire -- subjection and order.
questions.explanation: This threefold scheme is the organizing idea of the chapter's opening and frames Russell's later, more favourable judgment of Roman rule in Chapter XXIX.

questions.prompt: How, according to Russell, did Alexander's own policies help create the idea of 'mankind as a whole' before any philosopher formulated it in theory?
questions.answer: By deliberately promoting fusion between Greeks and non-Greeks -- marrying Persian princesses himself, compelling his officers to marry Persian noblewomen, and founding cities with intermarried, mixed populations -- Alexander broke down the old Greek assumption of superiority over 'barbarians,' making possible the later Stoic doctrine of cosmopolitanism.
questions.explanation: Russell is careful to say this cosmopolitan outlook 'begins in philosophy with the Stoics, but in practice it begins earlier, with Alexander' -- practice preceding theory.

questions.prompt: Contrast the political and intellectual role of a capable man in classical Athens (fifth-fourth centuries B.C.) with his role in the Hellenistic third century, as Russell describes it.
questions.answer: In classical Athens a capable man was expected to be soldier, politician, lawgiver, and philosopher by turns (Russell's examples: Socrates, Protagoras, Plato, Xenophon, Pythagorean mathematicians). In the Hellenistic third century, roles became specialized and separate -- soldiers, administrators, physicians, mathematicians, philosophers each occupied their own lane, and 'there was no one who was all these at once.'
questions.explanation: Russell attributes this shift to the loss of real political stakes in the old City States, which had become parochial under Macedonian military domination.

questions.prompt: What two, logically inconsistent, popular beliefs does Russell say Hellenistic people commonly held at the same time in response to their era's chronic insecurity?
questions.answer: Belief in the goddess Fortune (Tyche), i.e. arbitrary blind chance, and belief in astrology, i.e. a rigid, predictable cosmic Fate -- Russell notes 'most men believed in both, and never noticed the inconsistency.'
questions.explanation: This detail illustrates Russell's broader claim that intellectual confusion accompanied the era's political confusion.

questions.prompt: Which classical philosopher does Russell quote as expressing the ordinary Greek view that only Greeks combine 'spirit' and 'civilization,' an attitude Alexander's fusion policy began to undermine?
questions.explanation: Russell cites Aristotle's remark that northern races are spirited, southern races civilized, but only the Greeks are both, as representative of pre-Alexander Greek chauvinism.

questions.prompt: Reconstruct Russell's argument for why the disorder of the Hellenistic (Macedonian) age was, in his judgment, worse than either the earlier freedom of the Greek city-states or the later subjection to Rome.
questions.answer: Premise 1: The old Greek city-state disorder, though real, was tolerable because every citizen shared in political life and its risks. Premise 2: Hellenistic disorder was imposed on subject populations by incompetent, foreign Macedonian rulers who shared no power with them. Premise 3: Powerlessness combined with instability is worse than instability combined with participation. Conclusion: The Macedonian age's disorder was 'far more' intolerable than the subsequent, more orderly Roman subjection, even though Rome was 'stupid and brutal' by comparison to the Greeks.
questions.explanation: This argument explains why Russell can later (Ch. XXIX) treat Roman rule relatively favourably despite its being a loss of Greek self-government.

flashcards.back: Free City States (freedom + disorder) -> Macedonian/Hellenistic domination (subjection + disorder) -> Roman Empire (subjection + order).

flashcards.front: What Hellenistic city became the leading center of Greek mathematics and science?
flashcards.back: Alexandria, home to Euclid's tradition, Eratosthenes (chief librarian), and closely linked to Archimedes and Aristarchus.

flashcards.front: What historical policy of Alexander does Russell credit with creating cosmopolitanism 'in practice' before the Stoics created it 'in theory'?
flashcards.back: His deliberate fusion of Greek and non-Greek populations, including his own and his officers' marriages to Persian noblewomen.

flashcards.front: What classical ideal of the all-round citizen does Russell say the Hellenistic age abandoned?
flashcards.back: The idea that one capable man could be soldier, politician, lawgiver, and philosopher at once (as Socrates, Xenophon, and Plato had been, in different combinations).

flashcards.front: Which two popular beliefs about the future did most Hellenistic people hold simultaneously and inconsistently?
flashcards.back: Belief in the goddess Fortune (blind chance) and belief in astrological Fate (rigid determinism).

Free City States -> Macedonian domination -> Roman Empire
Macedonian domination -> Free City States -> Roman Empire

quiz.prompt: Which city became the pre-eminent center of Hellenistic mathematics and science, according to Russell?
quiz.explanation: Alexandria, capital of the Ptolemies, attracted Eratosthenes, Euclid's tradition, and was closely tied to Archimedes and Aristarchus.

quiz.prompt: In Russell's account, what practical policy of Alexander's laid the groundwork, in practice, for the later Stoic doctrine of cosmopolitanism?
options: His foundation of the Library of Alexandria
His deliberate promotion of intermarriage and fusion between Greeks and non-Greeks
His adoption of Persian court dress
His prosecution of Aristarchus of Samos
quiz.explanation: Russell explicitly credits Alexander's marriage policy and fusion of populations with beginning cosmopolitanism 'in practice,' before the Stoics formulated it in theory.
quiz.related_concept: Cosmopolitanism (the idea of mankind as a whole)

quiz.prompt: Which two popular beliefs does Russell say Hellenistic people commonly, and inconsistently, held together?
options: Belief in Fortune (Tyche) and belief in astrological Fate
quiz.explanation: Russell notes that most people believed simultaneously in arbitrary Luck and in a rigidly predictable astrological Fate, without noticing the contradiction.

quiz.prompt: Why does Russell judge the disorder of the Hellenistic (Macedonian) age to have been worse in practice than the disorder of the earlier free Greek city-states, even though both were periods of political instability?
options: Because Macedonian armies were less well organized than Greek hoplite forces
Because the earlier disorder was shared by citizens with a stake in it, while the later disorder was imposed on powerless subjects by incompetent rulers
Because Macedonian kings persecuted philosophers more severely
Because the earlier disorder had never involved warfare
quiz.explanation: Russell's argument turns on participation: disorder shared among free citizens is tolerable, disorder imposed on subjects with no power is not.

quiz.explanation: The quotation (from C. F. Angus) frames Hellenistic philosophy as therapeutic rather than exploratory -- picking up 'the weak and wounded.'

quiz.prompt: Which four schools of philosophy does Russell say were founded 'about the time of Alexander'?
quiz.explanation: These four schools -- treated across Chapters XXVI-XXVIII -- are the philosophical products of the Hellenistic collapse of the city-state.
